record.context_brief: Experimental reality of the paradox of enrichment
record.original_question: Is the paradox of enrichment a genuine experimentally observable ecological phenomenon, in which increasing the nutrient-driven carrying capacity of a prey population can lead to extinction of both prey and predator, or is it merely an artifact of a particular class of predator-prey mathematical models? If it is only a modeling artifact, then the underlying question becomes how to formulate better mathematical models that do not produce this spurious prediction while still capturing the ecological dynamics.

evidence.quote: Here we mention a few major open problems: 1. an effective description of chaos and turbulence, 2. rough dependence on initial data, 3. arrow of time, 4. the paradox of enrichment

The most important question is whether or not this paradox can be observed experimentally. It is possible that the paradox is purely an artifact of the mathematical models, while in reality increasing the nutrition to the prey never leads to an extinction. If that is the case, then developing better mathematical models is necessary.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a predator–prey ecological system. In a broad class of mathematical models (for example, Rosenzweig–MacArthur type ODE systems with logistic prey growth of carrying capacity K and Holling type II functional response), it is predicted that increasing K (the nutrient-driven carrying capacity of the prey) destabilizes the coexistence equilibrium via a Hopf bifurcation, producing limit cycles of growing amplitude that ultimately drive both prey and predator to extinction. This prediction is known as the paradox of enrichment.

Question: Is the paradox of enrichment a genuine ecological phenomenon that can be reliably reproduced in controlled experiments and observed in natural ecosystems—i.e., does sufficiently enriching the prey's nutrient supply, and thereby raising its carrying capacity, generically lead to extinction of both prey and predator? Or is the paradox purely an artifact of a particular class of predator–prey mathematical models? In the latter case, formulate a class of mathematical models for predator–prey dynamics that retain the essential ecological features (including density-dependent prey growth and saturating predator functional response) but do not exhibit the enrichment-induced extinction, and justify why such models are biologically more faithful.
artifact.status_search_result: The status is mixed and remains debated. Small-scale laboratory experiments (e.g., Luckinbill's and Veilleux's Didinium–Paramecium studies) provide limited support, while field evidence is weak; Jensen and Ginzburg argued most natural examples are inadequate. Numerous mathematical "resolutions" have been proposed (inedible/invulnerable/unpalatable prey, spatial refuges, predator–prey trait evolution, ratio-dependent functional responses, food-web complexity, fractional-order memory effects, and dimensional analyses of carrying capacity vs. half-saturation). No single resolution is universally accepted, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a resolution based on a dimensionless number formed from carrying capacity and prey half-saturation.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple mathematical resolutions have been proposed.

status_evidence.title: Unpalatable prey resolves the paradox of enrichment
status_evidence.snippet: Unpalatable prey may have stabilizing effects on predator-prey dynamics.
status_evidence.claim: Model modifications can eliminate the paradox.

status_evidence.title: The paradox of enrichment in an adaptive world
status_evidence.snippet: Trait evolution of predator or prey can stabilize the system.
